title: God's last word: the Son
sum: Hebrews begins without a greeting, like a sermon, with one long sentence (1:1-4) that tells the whole story in miniature: God spoke in the past in many pieces through the prophets, and has now spoken in a Son. The Son is heir of all things and the one through whom the ages were made. He is the brightness of God's glory and the exact stamp of his being, he carries all things along, he made a cleansing for sins, and he took his seat at God's right hand. Creator, revealer, priest and king are named before the word 'priest' appears.

The rest of the chapter (1:5-14) strings together seven Old Testament quotations, mostly from the Psalms, to show that the Son is 'better than the angels'. God never said to an angel 'You are my son'; the angels are told to bow down to him; they are winds and flames, while the Son's throne lasts forever; he made the earth and will outlast it; he sits at God's right hand while the angels are sent out as servants. The point matters because, as 2:2 says, the law was given through angels: if the Son is greater than they, his word is greater than theirs.
readings: Read as worship

The seven quotations read like a coronation: the king is declared Son, the court of heaven bows, his throne is proclaimed eternal, and he is seated at the right hand. Many readers hear in the chapter the worship of the early church, which sang psalms about Christ (Colossians 3:16).
Read as an argument

The chapter is also a careful argument from Scripture, built as a Jewish teacher would build it: each text is chosen for a word ('son', 'firstborn', 'angels', 'throne', 'Lord', 'sit') and the texts are set side by side to make one conclusion. The conclusion is practical, and 2:1 draws it at once: listen to the Son.
Read with Jewish eyes

Each quotation was, in its first setting, about Israel's God or Israel's king. Jewish readers hear Psalm 2, 2 Samuel 7 and Psalm 45 as royal texts about David's line, and Psalm 102 as addressed to God alone. Hebrews reads them as the Son's, because it believes the king of David's line has come and that he shares God's own name and work.

views.H: The readers had been believers for some time (5:12) and were under pressure. A sermon that begins by setting the Son above angels may answer a community that honored angels highly, as much of Judaism in that period did (the law given through angels, angelic princes of the nations), or simply prepares the argument of 2:1-4.
views.C: Critical scholars note that 1:1-4 has the rhythm of an early Christian hymn or creed, like Philippians 2:6-11, Colossians 1:15-20 and John 1:1-18; whether the writer used an existing hymn is debated. The Christology is among the highest in the New Testament, and the quotation at 1:6 follows a Greek form of Deuteronomy 32:43: the traditional Hebrew lacks the line, the Greek of Deuteronomy in Swete's edition words it differently, and the copy of the Song of Moses among the Odes printed after the Psalms matches it exactly (see the note).
views.L: The prologue is a single, balanced period, with alliteration in its first words and a careful rhythm. The chain of seven quotations moves from the Son's name (1:5) to his worship (1:6), his eternal throne (1:8-9), his creating work (1:10-12) and his session (1:13), and ends with a question that turns to the angels' role (1:14). The first and last quotations are introduced by the same question, 'Did he ever say to any one of the angels...?', framing the chain.
views.J: The chapter uses Jewish ways of reading: chains of texts joined by a key word, and the conviction that God's word to David's son belongs to the Messiah. The idea of God's Wisdom as the 'radiance' of his light (Wisdom of Solomon 7:26) and the agent of creation (Proverbs 8:22-31) lies behind 1:2-3. Jewish readers have always objected that Psalm 45 and Psalm 102 address a human king and God respectively, not a divine Son.
views.T: The fourth-century church used 1:3 against Arius: Athanasius argued that because the Son is the radiance of the Father's glory, there was never a time when he was not, as light is never without its brightness. The Nicene Creed's 'Light from Light' echoes the verse. 1:8 ('Your throne, O God') became one of the standard texts for the deity of Christ.

deep.b:
The chain is built with care:

1:5a Psalm 2:7, a coronation psalm: 'You are my son. This day I have fathered you.'
1:5b 2 Samuel 7:14, Nathan's promise to David: 'I will be a father to him.'
1:6 Deuteronomy 32:43 in a Greek form (compare Psalm 97:7): 'Let all the angels of God bow down to him.'
1:7 Psalm 104:4 in Greek: 'He makes his angels into winds.'
1:8-9 Psalm 45:6-7, a royal wedding song: 'Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever.'
1:10-12 Psalm 102:25-27 in Greek: 'At the start, Lord, you set the earth on its foundations.'
1:13 Psalm 110:1: 'Sit at my right hand.'

Three are about the Son as king (1:5, 8-9, 13), one about his worship (1:6), one about creation and eternity (1:10-12), and one about the angels' place (1:7). The last, Psalm 110:1, leads into the book's main text, Psalm 110:4, from 5:6 on.

deep.title: Claude's theory: an enthronement in seven scenes
deep.b: Claude's theory. The seven quotations may follow the order of an ancient royal enthronement as Psalm 2 and Psalm 110 picture it: the declaration of sonship (1:5), the presentation of the heir to the court (1:6, 'when he leads the firstborn in'), the court's homage (1:6-7), the acclamation of the throne and the anointing (1:8-9), the praise of the king's works (1:10-12), and the seating at the right hand (1:13). On this reading 'when he leads the firstborn into the world' (1:6) is the exaltation after the cross, not the birth at Bethlehem, which fits 1:3-4 ('he took his seat... he became better than the angels'). The theory builds on the exaltation reading of 1:6, one of the three readings set out in the note on that verse; the order of the seven scenes is Claude's own suggestion.

echoes: Psalm 2:7; 2 Samuel 7:14; Deuteronomy 32:43; Psalm 97:7; Psalm 104:4; Psalm 45:6-7; Psalm 102:25-27; Psalm 110:1; John 1:1-18; Colossians 1:15-20; Philippians 2:6-11; Wisdom of Solomon 7:26

settings.what: The opening of the sermon (the prologue)
settings.by: The unnamed writer of Hebrews, who speaks as 'we' and 'I' (2:3; 5:11; 6:9; 11:32; 13:19-23) and knows Timothy
settings.to: A Christian community the writer knew well, whose members had heard the gospel from eyewitnesses (2:3), had once suffered loss and insult for it (10:32-34), and were now growing tired and tempted to drift back (2:1; 5:11; 10:25)
settings.when: at the start of a sermon meant to be read aloud to the gathered church; written before about AD 96, many think before AD 70 and others between 70 and 90 (see the book page)
settings.why: To set the frame for everything that follows: God has spoken his final word in the Son, who is above every earlier messenger. Before any warning or argument, the readers hear who Jesus is: the heir, the creator, the image of God, the priest who cleansed sins, the king at God's right hand. Knowing that these readers were tired and under pressure changes the reading: the prologue is not abstract doctrine but a reason to keep listening (2:1).
views: Many read the readers as Jewish Christians, perhaps in Rome, tempted to return to the synagogue and the temple worship whose priests, sacrifices and covenant the sermon compares with Christ's.

Others think the readers were a mixed congregation, Jews and Gentiles, who had learned the Greek Old Testament in church, and whose danger was general weariness and fear of persecution, not a pull toward Judaism in particular.

settings.what: The seven quotations: the Son above the angels
settings.by: The unnamed writer of Hebrews, who speaks as 'we' and 'I' (2:3; 5:11; 6:9; 11:32; 13:19-23) and knows Timothy
settings.to: The same congregation, who knew the Greek Old Testament well enough to follow a chain of quotations
settings.when: right after the prologue, as the first proof
settings.why: To show from Scripture that the Son is greater than the angels, through whom the law came (2:2). The readers are meant to conclude that the message spoken through the Son demands even more attention than the law of Sinai. If some among them honored angels too highly, the chain also puts the angels in their place: servants sent for the sake of those who will inherit salvation (1:14).
views: Some think the readers were drawn to a teaching that exalted angels, as at Colossae (Colossians 2:18), or that saw the Messiah as an angel.
Setting up the argument about the law
Most think the comparison serves the point of 2:1-4: the law came through angels, the gospel through the Son.

title: Made like his brothers
sum: The first warning (2:1-4) comes straight out of chapter 1: if the law spoken through angels was binding, and every transgression was punished, then the message spoken through the Lord himself must be heard all the more. The danger is not open revolt but drift, slowly floating away from what they heard.

Then Hebrews turns to Psalm 8 (2:5-9). God made human beings a little below the angels and set everything under their feet; yet we do not see that. What we do see is Jesus, who was set below the angels for a while, suffered death for everyone and is now crowned with glory and honor. In 2:10-18 the writer explains why he had to suffer: to lead many sons to glory he had to share their blood and flesh, die, break the devil's grip on death and free those enslaved by fear. So he became like his brothers in every way, to be 'a merciful and faithful high priest' and to make atonement for the people's sins. That phrase announces the theme of the whole sermon.
readings: Read as the story of humanity

Psalm 8 describes what human beings were made for: glory, honor and rule over creation. Hebrews admits that this is not what we see, and finds the psalm fulfilled in Jesus, the true human, who goes first through suffering into glory and brings his brothers and sisters with him.
Read as the story of the Son

The Son of chapter 1, above the angels, comes down below them, shares flesh and blood, dies and is raised. Chapter 2 is the downward half of the movement Philippians 2:6-11 describes, and the reason Hebrews can call him both Son of God and brother of humans.

views.H: A congregation that had suffered loss (10:32-34) and feared worse would hear 2:14-15 directly: the fear of death keeps people enslaved, and Christ has broken it. The 'signs and wonders' of 2:4 were part of their own memory of how the gospel came to them.
views.C: The writer counts himself among those who heard the gospel from eyewitnesses (2:3), which most scholars take as evidence that he was not Paul. The quotation of Psalm 8 follows the Greek ('angels') against the Hebrew ('God'), and the reading 'apart from God' at 2:9 is one of the most debated variants in the letter (see the variants).
views.L: Hebrews alternates teaching and warning; 2:1-4 is the first warning, short and built on an argument 'from lesser to greater' (if the lesser was binding, how much more the greater). In 2:10-18 the key words are 'brothers', 'children', 'blood and flesh', 'like', leading to the climax 'high priest'.
views.J: Jewish tradition held that angels helped give the law at Sinai (Deuteronomy 33:2 Greek; Jubilees 1; Josephus), and that angels were set over the nations (Deuteronomy 32:8 Greek; Daniel 10). The phrase 'the world to come' echoes Jewish talk of this age and the age to come. 'Abraham's offspring' (2:16) names the people of the promise.
views.T: The church read 2:14-17 as one of the clearest texts on the incarnation: the Son took real flesh and blood in order to die. The early 'Christ the victor' picture of the atonement draws on 2:14-15, and 2:17 gave the language of Christ as the high priest who makes atonement.

deep.h: Why does Hebrews talk so much about angels?
deep.b:
Chapters 1-2 mention angels eleven times. Readers have given several reasons. (1) The law came through angels (2:2; Acts 7:53; Galatians 3:19), so setting the Son above angels sets the gospel above the law of Sinai. This is the reason Hebrews itself states. (2) Angels were honored, perhaps too much. Colossians 2:18 warns against 'the worship of angels', and some Jewish groups pictured exalted angelic mediators. (3) The world to come. This age was thought to be governed in part by angels (Deuteronomy 32:8 Greek; Daniel 10:13, 20); Hebrews says the next one is not (2:5).

Hebrews does not run angels down. They worship the Son (1:6), serve God's people (1:14) and fill the heavenly city (12:22); some have been entertained as guests without anyone knowing it (13:2).

echoes: Psalm 8:4-6; Psalm 22:22; Isaiah 8:17-18; Acts 7:53; Galatians 3:19; Philippians 2:6-11; 1 Corinthians 15:25-27; Mark 9:1; Mark 14:32-42; Romans 8:29

settings.what: The first warning: do not drift away
settings.by: The unnamed writer of Hebrews, who speaks as 'we' and 'I' (2:3; 5:11; 6:9; 11:32; 13:19-23) and knows Timothy
settings.to: A Christian community the writer knew well, whose members had heard the gospel from eyewitnesses (2:3), had once suffered loss and insult for it (10:32-34), and were now growing tired and tempted to drift back (2:1; 5:11; 10:25)
settings.when: after the chain of quotations about the Son
settings.why: To turn teaching into a call to listen. The readers were not yet in open revolt; the danger was slow drift. By reminding them that the gospel came to them with signs, wonders and gifts of the Spirit, the writer calls them back to what they themselves had seen. The first warning is mild; later ones grow sharper (6:4-8; 10:26-31; 12:25-29).
views: Many read the readers as Jewish Christians, perhaps in Rome, tempted to return to the synagogue and the temple worship whose priests, sacrifices and covenant the sermon compares with Christ's.

Others think the readers were a mixed congregation, Jews and Gentiles, who had learned the Greek Old Testament in church, and whose danger was general weariness and fear of persecution, not a pull toward Judaism in particular.

settings.what: Psalm 8 and the brothers: why the Son had to suffer
settings.by: The unnamed writer of Hebrews, who speaks as 'we' and 'I' (2:3; 5:11; 6:9; 11:32; 13:19-23) and knows Timothy
settings.to: The same congregation, who may have been troubled that their Lord died a shameful death and that they themselves were suffering
settings.why: To answer the scandal of the cross and of their own suffering. If Jesus is above the angels, why did he die? Because God's plan for human beings (Psalm 8) is fulfilled through suffering: the Son shared their humanity, died, broke death's power and became a high priest who knows their trials from the inside (2:18). For readers afraid of what their faith might cost, this was both an explanation and a comfort.
views: Most read 2:14-18 as pastoral: the readers' fear of death and their trials are met by a high priest who went through the same.
Some see an answer to Jewish objections that a crucified man could not be the Messiah (compare 1 Corinthians 1:23).

title: Today, if you hear his voice
sum: Hebrews now compares Jesus with the greatest figure of Israel's history, Moses. Both were faithful in God's house, as God himself said of Moses (Numbers 12:7). But Moses was faithful 'in' the house as an attendant, a witness to things still to come, while Christ is faithful 'over' the house as a Son. And the house is the readers themselves, 'if we hold on to our boldness and to the pride we take in our hope' (3:6).

That 'if' opens the second and longest warning (3:7-4:13), a sermon on Psalm 95:7-11. The psalm remembers Israel in the wilderness: rescued from Egypt, fed and led for forty years, and still they hardened their hearts, quarreled with God and tested him, and the whole generation died outside the land. 'Today', says the Holy Spirit, the same choice is open. The readers are to urge each other on every day, so that no one is tricked by sin, because 'we have become partners of Christ, as long as we keep the confidence we began with steady until the end' (3:14).
readings: Read as typology

The wilderness generation is a pattern for the church: both were rescued, both are on the way to a promised rest, both can fail through unbelief. Paul reads the same story the same way in 1 Corinthians 10:1-13.
Read as a sermon on a text
3:7-4:13 is a model of early Christian preaching: a psalm is quoted, and then its phrases ('Today', 'hear his voice', 'harden', 'forty years', 'swore', 'my rest') are taken up one by one and applied.
Read with Jewish eyes

Moses is honored here, not attacked; his faithfulness is quoted from God's own mouth. Jewish readers note that the comparison still places Moses below Jesus, and that Psalm 95 was a call to Israel to listen to the God of the covenant, which they understand as listening to the Torah.

views.H: A church whose members were growing tired, some skipping meetings (10:25), would hear Israel's story as their own: they had come out of their 'Egypt' and were in danger of falling short on the way. 'Encourage one another every day' assumes small house churches where members knew each other.
views.C: The writer follows the Greek of Psalm 95 (94 in Greek), which turns the place names Meribah and Massah into common nouns, and he moves 'forty years' to a new position, then adds 'So' (3:9-10), a deliberate change to the text he quotes. Critical scholars see in such handling the methods of Jewish interpretation of the time.
views.L: 3:1-6 is built on contrasts: servant and son, in and over, house and builder. 3:12-19 is a run of rhetorical questions (who? whom? to whom?) that drive home that the whole generation failed.
views.J: Moses as God's faithful servant (Numbers 12:7) was a central Jewish theme. The wilderness generation's failure is told in Numbers 14, and Psalm 95 was itself already a sermon on it. Hebrews' reading of 'rest' draws on Jewish associations of the land, the temple and the Sabbath.
views.T: The warning passages, beginning here, have been central to Christian debates on whether believers can fall away (see the card on chapter 6).

deep.h: Psalm 95 in Greek and in Hebrew
deep.b:
Hebrews quotes the Greek, which differs from the Hebrew in ways that matter:

Names become words. The Hebrew has 'as at Meribah, like that day in the wilderness at Massah'; the Greek has 'as in the embitterment, on the day of the testing'. The Plain English Translation writes 'the Bitter Quarrel' and 'the Testing' with capitals to show they were names.

Forty years moves. In the psalm the forty years belong to God's disgust; in Hebrews 3:9-10 they belong to Israel watching God's works, and a 'So' follows. In 3:17 Hebrews uses the psalm's own order.

'This generation'. The critical text of Hebrews has 'this generation', the psalm 'that generation' (see the variant).

David. The Greek Psalter gives the psalm a title naming David; the Hebrew has none. Hebrews 4:7 says God spoke 'in David'.

echoes: Numbers 12:7; Psalm 95:7-11; Exodus 17:1-7; Numbers 14:1-35; Numbers 20:1-13; 1 Corinthians 10:1-13; 2 Samuel 7:11-16; 1 Peter 2:5

settings.what: Moses the attendant, Christ the Son
settings.by: The unnamed writer of Hebrews, who speaks as 'we' and 'I' (2:3; 5:11; 6:9; 11:32; 13:19-23) and knows Timothy
settings.to: 'Holy brothers, partners in a calling from heaven' (3:1): the congregation, addressed for the first time directly
settings.when: after the theme of 'a merciful and faithful high priest' is announced (2:17); this section takes up 'faithful'
settings.why: To honor Moses and show that Jesus is greater still. For readers who loved the law, or who were tempted to fall back on it, this matters: they are not leaving Moses behind by following Jesus, since Moses was a witness to things that would be spoken later (3:5). And the faithful Son over the house calls for a faithful house: 'that house is us, if we hold on'.
views: Many read the readers as Jewish Christians, perhaps in Rome, tempted to return to the synagogue and the temple worship whose priests, sacrifices and covenant the sermon compares with Christ's.

Others think the readers were a mixed congregation, Jews and Gentiles, who had learned the Greek Old Testament in church, and whose danger was general weariness and fear of persecution, not a pull toward Judaism in particular.

settings.what: The second warning: a sermon on Psalm 95
settings.by: The unnamed writer of Hebrews, who speaks as 'we' and 'I' (2:3; 5:11; 6:9; 11:32; 13:19-23) and knows Timothy
settings.to: A Christian community the writer knew well, whose members had heard the gospel from eyewitnesses (2:3), had once suffered loss and insult for it (10:32-34), and were now growing tired and tempted to drift back (2:1; 5:11; 10:25)
settings.when: right after the comparison with Moses, whose generation is the example
settings.why: To make the readers see themselves in Israel's wilderness generation: rescued, on the way, and in danger of falling short through unbelief. 'Today' turns an old psalm into God's present call. The writer wants a church that warns and encourages its members every day, and that fears missing God's rest more than it fears the cost of faith.
views: Many read the section as aimed at a real danger: some members were close to leaving the faith.
Others think the writer paints the danger in strong colors to stir a basically faithful church (compare 6:9).

title: The rest that remains
sum: Chapter 4 finishes the sermon on Psalm 95 by asking what 'my rest' means. It cannot be only the land of Canaan: Joshua led Israel in, and yet centuries later, in David's time, God still said 'Today... do not harden your hearts.' It is God's own rest, the rest he entered on the seventh day of creation, which Genesis never says ended. So 'a Sabbath rest is still waiting for God's people' (4:9), and the readers must be eager to enter it, so that no one falls the way Israel fell.

The warning closes with a picture of God's word as a living sword that reaches to the depths of a person, and of God's eyes from which nothing is hidden (4:12-13). Then the tone turns at once to comfort: 'We have a great high priest' who has gone through the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, who can feel for us in our weaknesses because he was tested in every way as we are, but without sin. So let us come near to the throne of grace with boldness (4:14-16). These three verses begin the central part of the book, about Jesus the high priest.
readings: Rest as the world to come
Most readers take the rest as the final inheritance of God's people, the heavenly homeland of 11:13-16 and the city of 12:22-24, which believers enter fully at the end and are already on the way to.
Rest as present peace
Others stress the present tense of 4:3 ('we are going into rest') and read the rest as begun now, in trust in God, ceasing from the attempt to make oneself right with him.
Rest as Sabbath

The word sabbatismos (4:9) keeps the weekly Sabbath in view. Christians differ on how the Sabbath command applies to them; Hebrews uses the Sabbath as a picture of God's final rest, not as a rule about days.

views.H: For a community that had lost property and security (10:34), the promise of rest was concrete. Ancient listeners heard the sermon read aloud; 4:12-13 would have come as a solemn close to a long warning.
views.C: Critical scholars note the Jewish method behind 4:3-5: two passages that share a word ('rest' in Psalm 95:11 and Genesis 2:2 Greek) are read together to explain each other. The rare word sabbatismos and the double meaning of the name Iēsous (Joshua and Jesus, 4:8) are part of the writer's careful craft.
views.L: The section is framed by 'let us fear' (4:1) and 'let us be eager' (4:11), and closes with the sword image and a pun on logos, 'word' and 'account' (4:12-13). 4:14-16 balances 'let us keep a strong hold' with 'let us come near'.
views.J: Rest (menuchah) in the Hebrew Bible is the land (Deuteronomy 12:9), the temple (Psalm 132:14) and the Sabbath (Exodus 20:11). Hebrews shares the hope of a final rest and finds its door in Christ.
views.T: 4:12 has been used by Christians in every tradition as a text about Scripture. 4:15 is a standard text for the sinlessness of Christ. The Council of Chalcedon (451), answering the 'one-nature' teaching of Eutyches, confessed Christ 'like us in all things, sin apart'; the Catholic and Orthodox churches, and with them most Protestant churches, accept that definition, while the Oriental Orthodox churches do not accept the council.

deep.b:
Hebrews 3-4 layers three kinds of rest:

The land. The 'rest' Israel failed to enter in the wilderness (Numbers 14; Deuteronomy 12:9). Joshua brought the next generation in (Joshua 21:44), but not into the final rest (4:8).

God's own rest. 'On the seventh day God rested from all his works' (Genesis 2:2). Since then God's rest has stood open (4:3-4).

The Sabbath rest still waiting. 'A Sabbath rest is still waiting for God's people' (4:9): the share in God's rest that the readers are urged to enter, now by faith and fully at the end.

The argument from 'Today' (4:7) is about time: if David, long after Joshua, still spoke of entering God's rest, then the land was only a picture of something greater.

echoes: Psalm 95:7-11; Genesis 2:2-3; Joshua 21:44; Deuteronomy 12:9; Exodus 16:30; Isaiah 49:2; Revelation 1:16; Matthew 11:28-29; 2 Corinthians 5:21; Leviticus 16:2

settings.what: The high priest who feels for us
settings.by: The unnamed writer of Hebrews, who speaks as 'we' and 'I' (2:3; 5:11; 6:9; 11:32; 13:19-23) and knows Timothy
settings.to: A Christian community the writer knew well, whose members had heard the gospel from eyewitnesses (2:3), had once suffered loss and insult for it (10:32-34), and were now growing tired and tempted to drift back (2:1; 5:11; 10:25)
settings.when: right after the long warning of 3:7-4:13, as its comfort; it takes up 'merciful' from 2:17
settings.why: To give tired believers a reason to keep coming to God: their high priest is not distant but has been tested as they are. The section sets out what makes a high priest (taken from among human beings, called by God) and shows that Jesus has both qualifications, being called by God's oath (Psalm 2:7; Psalm 110:4) and having learned obedience through suffering. For readers who might be drawn to the visible priesthood of the temple, it says: you have a high priest, a better one.
views: Many read the readers as Jewish Christians, perhaps in Rome, tempted to return to the synagogue and the temple worship whose priests, sacrifices and covenant the sermon compares with Christ's.

Others think the readers were a mixed congregation, Jews and Gentiles, who had learned the Greek Old Testament in church, and whose danger was general weariness and fear of persecution, not a pull toward Judaism in particular.

title: Called by God, after the pattern of Melchizedek
sum: Every high priest, Hebrews explains, is taken from among human beings to act for them before God, to offer gifts and sacrifices for sins. Because he is weak himself, he can be patient with those who sin out of ignorance, and he must offer for his own sins as well. And no one takes this honor for himself: God calls him, as he called Aaron (5:1-4). Christ meets both conditions in his own way: God, who said 'You are my son', also said 'You are a priest forever, after the pattern of Melchizedek' (5:5-6), and in the days of his flesh Christ cried out with tears to the one who could save him out of death, and learned obedience through what he suffered (5:7-8). Made perfect, he became the cause of eternal salvation (5:9-10).

Here the writer stops. He has much to say about Melchizedek, but his hearers have grown sluggish. They ought to be teachers by now, but they need milk again, not solid food. Solid food is for the grown-ups, whose senses are trained to tell good from bad (5:11-14). This rebuke opens the third warning, which runs to 6:20.
readings: Read as Gethsemane

Most readers hear in 5:7 the night in the garden, when Jesus prayed that the cup might pass (Mark 14:36). Hebrews shows a high priest who did not escape fear and grief, and whose prayer was answered by resurrection, not by being spared death.
Read as a portrait of a priest

5:1-10 compares Christ with Aaron point by point: from among humans, for humans, gentle with the ignorant, offering for sins, called by God. Christ fits each, except that he needs no offering for himself (7:27).

views.H: In the century before the readers, Herod the Great and the Roman governors appointed and removed high priests at will (Josephus, Antiquities 15.3.1; 18.2.2); the contrast with a high priest called by God's oath may have struck them. The rebuke of 5:11-14 suggests a community that had been believers for years.
views.C: 5:7 is often taken as independent evidence for the tradition of Jesus' agony before his death. Whether it rests on the Gospel stories, on early tradition, or on psalms of lament (Psalm 22:24) is debated. The puzzle 'he was heard' has produced different readings and one modern conjecture (see the note).
views.L: The section 5:1-10 is built in mirror order: the qualifications are stated (solidarity, then calling) and then fulfilled in reverse (calling, then solidarity). The wordplay emathen / epathen ('learned / suffered', 5:8) and the frame 'sluggish' (5:11; 6:12) show the writer's craft.
views.J: The portrait of the high priest comes from Leviticus (4; 9:7; 16), and the call from Exodus 28:1 and Numbers 16-17. Psalm 110:4's priest 'after the pattern of Melchizedek' was read in Jewish tradition too: the Talmud (Nedarim 32b) applies the verse to Abraham.
views.T: 5:7-8 has been central to discussions of Christ's two natures and wills: the Son, who is God, truly feared, prayed and learned obedience as a man. 5:12-14 has been used in Christian teaching about growth from basic to mature faith.

deep.b:
'Because of his reverence he was heard' (5:7) raises a hard question: Jesus prayed to be saved from death, and he died. Readers have answered in several ways.

(1) He was saved out of death. The Greek is ek thanatou, 'out of death': God answered not by sparing him death but by raising him from it.

(2) He was heard because he submitted. His prayer included 'not what I want, but what you want' (Mark 14:36), and that prayer was granted.

(3) He was heard and freed from fear. The KJV reads 'was heard in that he feared', and some take it that he was strengthened to go on (compare Luke 22:43).

(4) A changed text? Some have supposed that 'not' fell out of the text ('he was not heard'). James Swetnam, who surveys the proposals, answers that 'no manuscript has' it, and sets the plea at the cross, where Jesus prayed Psalm 22.

echoes: Exodus 28:1; Leviticus 9:7; Leviticus 16:6; Numbers 16-17; Psalm 2:7; Psalm 110:4; Mark 14:32-42; Luke 22:39-46; John 12:27; 1 Corinthians 3:1-2; Philippians 2:8

settings.what: The third warning begins: milk and solid food
settings.by: The unnamed writer of Hebrews, who speaks as 'we' and 'I' (2:3; 5:11; 6:9; 11:32; 13:19-23) and knows Timothy
settings.to: A Christian community the writer knew well, whose members had heard the gospel from eyewitnesses (2:3), had once suffered loss and insult for it (10:32-34), and were now growing tired and tempted to drift back (2:1; 5:11; 10:25)
settings.when: in the middle of the argument about Melchizedek, which the writer breaks off to rouse his hearers; the warning runs on to 6:12 and the anchor of hope to 6:20
settings.why: To wake up a church that had grown sluggish before the hardest part of the teaching. The writer shames them (by now you should be teachers) and calls them to leave the first lessons behind and be carried on to full growth. The purpose is not to condemn them but to move them on to maturity; the sharp warning that follows (6:4-8) is framed by this call and by the reassurance of 6:9-12.
views: A real danger in the church
Many think some members had already stopped meeting (10:25) and were close to leaving.
A warning to keep the faithful faithful
Others stress 6:9: the writer is sure of better things for them, and the warning is meant as a means of keeping them.

title: No way back, and an anchor behind the veil
sum: The writer urges his hearers to leave the beginning lessons behind and be carried on to full growth. Then comes the most debated warning in the letter: it is impossible to bring back to repentance those who once received the light, tasted the gift from heaven, shared in the Holy Spirit and tasted the powers of the age to come, and then fell away, crucifying the Son of God again for themselves (6:4-6). Like ground that drinks the rain and grows only thorns, such a life ends in the fire (6:7-8).

At once the tone changes: 'about you, beloved, we are persuaded of better things' (6:9). God will not forget their love and service. They are to imitate those who inherit the promises through faith and patience, like Abraham, to whom God made a promise and then swore by himself. God's promise and God's oath are two unchangeable things, and the hope they guarantee is an anchor for the soul, fixed behind the veil, where Jesus has gone ahead of us as high priest forever after the pattern of Melchizedek (6:13-20).
readings: Read as a warning to true believers

On this reading the people of 6:4-5 are genuine believers, and the passage teaches that a believer can fall away so completely that return becomes impossible. The warning is meant to keep the readers from that path.
Read as a warning about false believers

On this reading the people of 6:4-5 experienced much of the gospel's power in the church without being truly born again; their falling away shows what they were. True believers are kept by God, and the warning is one of the means by which he keeps them.
Read in the setting of early church practice
Many early readers took 'impossible to make them new again' as ruling out a second baptism, not a second repentance: the sinner can be restored by repentance but cannot be baptized again.

views.H: The readers had once been 'given the light', probably at baptism, and had shown love by serving fellow believers (6:10; 10:32-34). Some were growing slack. The warning about public shame (6:6) fits a setting where going back meant siding publicly with those who rejected Jesus.
views.C: The passage was one reason some in the Western church hesitated over Hebrews in the early centuries: it was used by rigorists to deny restoration to the fallen (see the note on 6:6). The Greek participles in 6:6 can be read as giving a reason or a time limit ('as long as they keep crucifying'), which affects the meaning.
views.L: The section is framed by 'sluggish' (5:11; 6:12). The warning (6:4-8) and the reassurance (6:9-12) are deliberately set side by side. The farming picture of 6:7-8 and the anchor of 6:19 give the abstract argument something to see.
views.J: The six foundations of 6:1-2 (repentance, faith in God, washings, laying on of hands, resurrection, judgment) all have Jewish roots. God's oath to Abraham after the binding of Isaac (Genesis 22:16-17) was central to Jewish hope, and the phrase 'the inner side of the veil' is taken from the Day of Atonement law (Leviticus 16:2, 12).
views.T: 6:4-6 divides the churches on whether believers can lose salvation and on what repentance after baptism means (see the card).

deep.b:
Hebrews alternates teaching with warnings, and the warnings grow sharper:

2:1-4 Do not drift away from what you heard.
3:7-4:13 Do not harden your hearts like the wilderness generation; be eager to enter God's rest.
5:11-6:12 You have grown sluggish; those who fall away cannot be brought back to repentance; but we are sure of better things for you.
10:26-39 If we keep on sinning by choice, no sacrifice for sins is left; do not throw away your confidence.
12:14-29 Do not be like Esau; do not turn away from the one who speaks from heaven.

Each warning is followed or surrounded by encouragement. Any reading of 6:4-6 has to account for 6:9-20 as well, and for the parallel in 10:26-39, which also ends 'we are not people of shrinking back' (10:39).

echoes: Genesis 22:16-17; Genesis 3:17-18; Isaiah 5:1-7; Leviticus 16:2; Numbers 35:9-28; Hebrews 10:26-39; Hebrews 12:15-17; Matthew 12:31-32; 2 Peter 2:20-22; 1 John 5:16

settings.what: The sharpest warning, and 'better things' for the readers
settings.by: The unnamed writer of Hebrews, a teacher who calls himself 'we' and knows his hearers' history (6:9-10; 10:32-34)
settings.to: A congregation that had once been 'given the light', probably at baptism, had served fellow believers and still did (6:10), but had grown slow to listen (5:11) and included some who were drifting from the meetings (10:25)
settings.when: right after the call to move on from the first lessons (6:1-3)
settings.why: To make the readers feel how serious it would be to turn their backs on what they had received, and then, at once, to assure them that he does not think this of them ('about you, beloved, we are persuaded of better things', 6:9). Knowing the hearers changes the reading: the warning is spoken to a church the writer loves and believes in, to keep it from a road he fears some may be starting down. How the warning applies to believers today is one of the questions that divide the churches; see the card.
views: A real danger for real believers
Many read the warning as addressed to genuine believers who could truly fall away, and who are being kept from it by being warned.
A warning about those who never belonged
Others read 6:4-8 as describing people who shared in the church's life without being reborn, while 6:9 assures the real believers among the hearers.

settings.what: God's oath to Abraham, the anchor of hope
settings.by: The unnamed writer of Hebrews, who speaks as 'we' and 'I' (2:3; 5:11; 6:9; 11:32; 13:19-23) and knows Timothy
settings.to: The same congregation, now called 'beloved' and reassured (6:9)
settings.when: right after the sharp warning and its reassurance, leading back to Melchizedek
settings.why: To give wavering believers solid ground. Abraham waited patiently and received what was promised; God guaranteed his promise with an oath. The readers are heirs of the same promise, and their hope is fastened where Jesus has already gone, behind the veil. The writer wants them to stop doubting God's faithfulness, not to doubt their own place in his promise.
views: Many read the readers as Jewish Christians, perhaps in Rome, tempted to return to the synagogue and the temple worship whose priests, sacrifices and covenant the sermon compares with Christ's.

Others think the readers were a mixed congregation, Jews and Gentiles, who had learned the Greek Old Testament in church, and whose danger was general weariness and fear of persecution, not a pull toward Judaism in particular.

traditions.q: Can someone who has truly believed fall away and be lost (6:4-6)? (This card also serves the parallel warnings in Hebrews 10:26-31 and 2 Peter 2:20-22. The churches listed are those whose confessions or chief teachers speak to the question directly; more readings are in the note on Hebrews 6:6.)
views: No. Those whom God has effectually called and sanctified 'can neither totally nor finally fall away from the state of grace; but shall certainly persevere therein to the end' (Westminster Confession 17.1). 'Neither does God let them fall down so far that they forfeit the grace of adoption and the state of justification' (Canons of Dort, fifth main point, article 6, in the translation adopted by the Christian Reformed Church in 2011). Calvin read 6:4-6 of 'a total defection or falling away from the Gospel', and held that the reprobate may have 'some knowledge' of the gospel 'which afterwards vanishes away'. Some Reformed and Baptist scholars, such as Thomas Schreiner and Ardel Caneday, read the warnings instead as 'the means God uses to save and preserve his people to the end'.

Baptists are divided. The Second London Baptist Confession (1689, 17.1), held by Reformed Baptists, teaches that those whom God has accepted 'can neither totally nor finally fall from the state of grace, but shall certainly persevere therein to the end'. Free Will Baptists teach the opposite: 'their future obedience and final salvation are neither determined nor certain, since through infirmity and manifold temptations they are in danger of falling; and they ought, therefore, to watch and pray lest they make shipwreck of their faith and be lost' (Treatise of the National Association of Free Will Baptists, chapter 13).

Yes, a believer can fall away. John Wesley wrote on 6:6: 'Here is not a supposition, but a plain relation of fact', describing people who had real faith, hope and love and then willfully cast them away. The Methodist Articles of Religion (12) add that 'we may depart from grace given, and fall into sin, and, by the grace of God, rise again and amend our lives'.

A justified person can lose grace. The Council of Trent condemned the claim that 'a man once justified can sin no more, nor lose grace' (session 6, canon 23) and taught that, 'except by special revelation, it cannot be known whom God hath chosen unto Himself' (chapter 12). Mortal sin 'results in the loss of charity and the privation of sanctifying grace' but can be 'redeemed by repentance and God's forgiveness' (Catechism 1861). On the verse itself, Thomas Aquinas wrote that it does not say 'that it is impossible to repent, but that it is impossible to be renewed again, i.e., baptized'.

Grace can be lost and restored. The Confession of Dositheus (1672) teaches that one rightly baptized cannot be baptized again even after apostasy, but 'when he is willing to return unto the Lord, he receives again through the Mystery of Penance the adoption of a son, which he had lost' (decree 16). John Chrysostom read 6:6 as excluding 'the renewing again by the laver' (a second baptism), not repentance.

The justified can lose the Holy Spirit and be restored. The Augsburg Confession (article 12) condemns 'the Anabaptists, who deny that those once justified can lose the Holy Ghost', and also condemns the Novatians, 'who would not absolve such as had fallen after Baptism'. Luther called the denial of repentance in Hebrews 6 and 10 'a hard knot'.

The Thirty-Nine Articles (16) teach that 'not every deadly sin willingly committed after Baptism is sin against the Holy Ghost, and unpardonable', and that 'after we have received the Holy Ghost, we may depart from grace given, and fall into sin, and by the grace of God we may arise again'.

title: A priest forever, after the pattern of Melchizedek
sum: At last the writer gives the 'solid food' (5:14): Melchizedek. Genesis says only that Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, met Abraham coming back from battle, blessed him and received a tenth of everything (Genesis 14:18-20). Hebrews reads every detail: his name means 'king of righteousness', his city 'peace'; Scripture gives him no father, mother or family tree, no birth and no death, so he stands as a likeness of the Son, a priest for all time. He is greater than Abraham, since Abraham gave him a tenth and received his blessing, and so greater than Levi, who was still in Abraham's body (7:1-10).

From this Hebrews draws a startling conclusion (7:11-28). If the Levitical priesthood could have brought people to perfection, why would God promise in Psalm 110:4 a different priest after a different pattern? A change of priesthood means a change of law, and Jesus came from Judah, not Levi. His priesthood rests not on descent but on 'the power of a life that can never be torn down', and it was sworn by God's oath. The old priests died and were replaced; he remains forever, and so he can save completely those who come near to God through him, since he always lives to plead for them. He needs no daily sacrifices: he offered himself once for all. The law appointed weak men; the oath appointed a Son, made perfect forever.
readings: Read as typology

Melchizedek is a real figure whom Scripture presents in such a way that he points to Christ: a priest-king, without recorded beginning or end, greater than Abraham. Hebrews' argument depends on what Genesis says and what it leaves unsaid.
Read against Jewish interpretation

Hebrews joins a lively Jewish conversation about Melchizedek: Philo made him a picture of reason and peace, the Qumran scroll 11QMelchizedek a heavenly deliverer, and the rabbis identified him with Shem. In the dominant Christian reading, Hebrews' Melchizedek is neither angel nor Shem but a likeness of the eternal Son, though some scholars hear the angelic Melchizedek of Qumran behind 7:3.
Read as an argument about the law

Chapter 7 is one of the strongest New Testament statements that the law of Moses, at least its priesthood, has been replaced. How far the 'change of law' (7:12) reaches is one of the questions that divide Christian traditions from one another and from Judaism.

views.H: The readers lived in a world where a high priest in Jerusalem still offered sacrifices (unless the letter was written after AD 70). For believers drawn to a visible priesthood, the argument says: you have a better priest, permanent, sinless, at God's right hand.
views.C: Scholars note that Hebrews reads Genesis 14 by Jewish methods: arguing from the meaning of names and from what Scripture does not say. The account of the high priest offering 'each day' (7:27) does not match Leviticus 16 exactly, and readers explain it in different ways (see the note).
views.L: Chapter 7 is framed by Psalm 110:4 and full of contrasts: many priests and one, dying and living, without oath and with oath, weakness and perfection, law and oath. It ends with three key words: 'a Son made perfect forever'.
views.J: Melchizedek was a figure of interest in Second Temple Judaism (11QMelchizedek, Philo, 2 Enoch) and in rabbinic tradition, which made him Shem and transferred his priesthood to Abraham (Bavli Nedarim 32b). Jewish readers object that the Torah gives Aaron's sons "a priesthood for all time" (Exodus 40:15) and that Hebrews' 'change of law' (7:12) is an argument they do not accept.
views.T: 7:23-28 is at the center of the debate about priesthood in the church: whether Christ's unique priesthood is shared by an ordained ministry (Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican) or leaves only the priesthood of all believers (most Protestants). See the card.

deep.b:
Genesis 14:18-20. The priest-king of Salem who brings bread and wine, blesses Abram and receives a tenth.

Psalm 110:4. The king of David's line is 'a priest forever, after the pattern of Melchizedek'.

11QMelchizedek (Qumran; composed, by the usual dating, about 100 BC). Melchizedek is a heavenly figure who leads God's angels, proclaims liberty to captives (Isaiah 61:1), brings atonement at the end of the tenth jubilee and judges with God; Psalm 82:1, 'God has taken his place in the divine council', is applied to him.

Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish philosopher who lived in the time of Jesus, calls him 'the king of peace' and 'a just king', and makes him a figure of reason as a priest.

2 Enoch 69-73 (date uncertain; in some manuscripts only) tells of a Melchizedek born miraculously to the wife of Noah's brother and taken to paradise before the flood.

The rabbis. The Targum Pseudo-Jonathan on Genesis 14:18 calls him 'Shem bar Noah, the king of Yerushalem' (J. W. Etheridge's translation, 1862); the Talmud (Nedarim 32b) says God meant the priesthood to come from him but gave it to Abraham because Melchizedek blessed Abraham before he blessed God.

Hebrews shares none of these speculations openly. Its Melchizedek is the Melchizedek of Genesis and the Psalm, read as a likeness of the Son.

echoes: Genesis 14:17-20; Psalm 110:4; Numbers 18:21-28; Leviticus 16:6-11; Leviticus 6:20; Numbers 24:17; Romans 8:34; Romans 6:10; 1 John 2:1; Isaiah 53:12; 11QMelchizedek

settings.by: The unnamed writer of Hebrews, who speaks as 'we' and 'I' (2:3; 5:11; 6:9; 11:32; 13:19-23) and knows Timothy
settings.to: A Christian community the writer knew well, whose members had heard the gospel from eyewitnesses (2:3), had once suffered loss and insult for it (10:32-34), and were now growing tired and tempted to drift back (2:1; 5:11; 10:25)
settings.when: after the warning and the anchor of hope; this is the 'solid food' promised in 5:11-14
settings.why: To show from Genesis that there is a priesthood older and greater than Levi's. For readers who honored Abraham and the Levitical priesthood, the argument is meant to persuade from within their own Scriptures: Abraham himself paid a tenth to Melchizedek and received his blessing.
views: Many read the readers as Jewish Christians, perhaps in Rome, tempted to return to the synagogue and the temple worship whose priests, sacrifices and covenant the sermon compares with Christ's.

Others think the readers were a mixed congregation, Jews and Gentiles, who had learned the Greek Old Testament in church, and whose danger was general weariness and fear of persecution, not a pull toward Judaism in particular.

settings.what: A new priest, a change of law, an oath
settings.by: The unnamed writer of Hebrews, who speaks as 'we' and 'I' (2:3; 5:11; 6:9; 11:32; 13:19-23) and knows Timothy
settings.to: A Christian community the writer knew well, whose members had heard the gospel from eyewitnesses (2:3), had once suffered loss and insult for it (10:32-34), and were now growing tired and tempted to drift back (2:1; 5:11; 10:25)
settings.why: To draw the consequence: the promise of a priest 'after the pattern of Melchizedek' means the Levitical priesthood was not final, and with it the law built on it has changed. Jesus' priesthood rests on an oath and on an indestructible life, so it is permanent and able to save completely. For readers tempted back to the old system, the message is that it could never do what Christ has done once for all.
views: Hearers who still saw the Temple's sacrifices
If the sermon was written before AD 70, the hearers knew priests who were still offering sacrifices in Jerusalem, and 7:27-28 set Christ against a living system they could see.
Hearers who had lost the Temple
If it was written after AD 70, the hearers had seen the Temple fall, and the chapter told them that its loss did not leave them without a priest or a sacrifice.

traditions.q: If Christ is the one high priest forever (7:23-28), is there still an ordained priesthood in the church? (What the priesthood of all believers is, and how it relates to ordained ministers, is the card at 1 Peter 2:5-9.)
views: Yes. 'Only Christ is the true priest, the others being only his ministers' (Catechism 1545), yet his one priesthood 'is made present through the ministerial priesthood without diminishing the uniqueness of Christ's priesthood'. The ministerial priesthood and 'the common priesthood of all the faithful' both share in Christ's priesthood, 'each in its own proper way', and 'they differ essentially' (1547). The Council of Trent taught that in the church there is 'a new, visible, and external priesthood, into which the old has been translated' (session 23, chapter 1). The Catechism calls Melchizedek 'a prefiguration of the priesthood of Christ' (1544).

Christ alone is priest, and the ordained share in his ministry. The Orthodox Church in America teaches that 'Christ is the only priest, pastor and teacher of the Christian Church' and that bishops, priests and deacons 'have no other function or service than to manifest the presence and action of Christ to his people'. The Confession of Dositheus (decree 16) holds that priesthood, like baptism, 'imparts an indelible character'.

Ministers are not sacrificing priests. The Apology of the Augsburg Confession (article 13) rejects a priesthood 'like the Levitical' that offers sacrifice for the people, since 'the sacrifice of Christ dying on the cross has been sufficient for the sins of the whole world'; ministers are called priests only to teach the gospel and give the sacraments. Luther taught that 'we are all consecrated as priests by baptism' (To the Christian Nobility, 1520).

Christ is the one 'mediator between God and men, the prophet, priest, and king' (Westminster Confession 8.1), who 'by His perfect obedience and sacrifice of Himself, which He through the eternal Spirit once offered up unto God, hath fully satisfied the justice of His Father' (8.5). The Heidelberg Catechism calls him 'our only high priest who has delivered us by the one sacrifice of his body' (answer 31), and says every Christian shares in his anointing, 'to present myself to him as a living sacrifice of thanks' (answer 32, citing 1 Peter 2:5, 9).

The Thirty-Nine Articles (31) call the offering of Christ 'once made' the 'perfect redemption, propitiation, and satisfaction, for all the sins of the whole world', and reject 'the sacrifices of Masses'. Yet the Ordinal of the Book of Common Prayer keeps the order of 'Priests' and gives the newly ordained 'the Office and Work of a Priest in the Church of God', to forgive sins in Christ's name and dispense the word and sacraments.
